claims.text: Controlled nanoscale chemical heterogeneity governs strong low-field magnetocaloric response in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
The relevant heterogeneity consists of magnetically soft nanoscale precipitates embedded in a mechanically robust matrix.
Magnetically soft nanoscale precipitates promote a rapid, nearly second-order magnetoelastic transition.
The precipitate-mediated magnetoelastic transition enhances magnetic entropy change.
The precipitate-mediated transition maintains rapid heat exchange and low hysteresis.
The starting alloy has a relatively homogeneous, coarse-grained microstructure with randomized elemental distribution.
Controlled annealing at approximately 800°C can induce nanoscale magnetically soft precipitates in the preexisting matrix.
Precipitate size and presence mediate the alloy's magnetocaloric properties.
Nanoscale precipitates enhance local magnetoelastic coupling.
Nanoscale precipitates improve thermal conductivity without significant mechanical or magnetic energy loss.
Soft magnetic precipitates alter the local balance between magnetic exchange interactions and elastic strain.
The altered exchange-strain balance encourages a low-field, nearly reversible magnetoelastic transition.
Nanostructuring minimizes the energy barriers responsible for hysteresis.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the annealed alloy will exhibit a larger magnetic entropy change under applied fields of 0–1 T.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the annealed alloy will exhibit significantly reduced magnetic hysteresis.
The annealed alloy will maintain or enhance mechanical stability because of improved heat-conduction paths.
The as-cast coarse-grained baseline has a weaker low-field magnetocaloric response, higher hysteresis, and less efficient heat exchange.
The hypothesis is expected to apply only where the alloy supports a robust-matrix/magnetically-soft-precipitate dual-phase microstructure and annealing avoids deleterious coarsening.
